report:
**Conclusion:** Your claim is supported by a high-quality randomized trial, but its scope is specific: exemestane reduced *new breast-cancer diagnoses* over short-term follow-up in postmenopausal women selected for elevated risk.

In the double-blind MAP.3 trial (4,560 women), invasive breast cancer occurred at an annual rate of 0.19% with exemestane versus 0.55% with placebo after a median 35 months (hazard ratio 0.35; 95% CI 0.18–0.70)—about a 65% relative reduction. Eligibility included age ≥60 or risk factors such as elevated calculated risk, atypical hyperplasia, or lobular carcinoma in situ. The result is particularly biologically plausible for estrogen-receptor-positive cancers because exemestane blocks estrogen synthesis.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1103507

Important qualifications: follow-up was short for a prevention intervention, so the trial did not establish reduced breast-cancer mortality or long-term net benefit. Aromatase inhibitors can cause menopausal/musculoskeletal symptoms and reduce bone mineral density; whether this translates into more fractures needs longer observation.  
https://www.cancer.gov/types/breast/research/exemestane-reduces-risk  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3354700/

Thus, exemestane is evidence-based as a risk-reducing option for appropriately selected postmenopausal women, not a universal preventive medication. Individual baseline cancer risk, bone health, symptoms, and alternatives should guide a clinician-patient decision.
